questions.s: Ayesha, 26, attends a BHU in rural Sindh for her first antenatal visit at 10 weeks of gestation. She is well. Which supplement should be started at this visit for all pregnant women according to WHO antenatal guidance?
o: Daily oral iron and folic acid
Daily oral calcium and vitamin K
questions.e: WHO recommends daily oral iron with folic acid for all pregnant women to prevent maternal anaemia, low birth weight and preterm birth. High-dose vitamin A is not recommended routinely in pregnancy because it is teratogenic in excess.

questions.s: Rukhsana, 30, gravida 2, is blood group O Rh-negative. Her first child is Rh-positive. Her indirect Coombs test at booking is negative. She is now 28 weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Repeat indirect Coombs test only at delivery
Arrange fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler
Give anti-D only if bleeding occurs
questions.e: A non-sensitised Rh-negative woman should receive routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis around 28 weeks, as silent fetomaternal haemorrhage can sensitise her in the third trimester. Middle cerebral artery Doppler is used to look for fetal anaemia in women already sensitised, which she is not.

questions.s: A 24-year-old primigravida has a regular 28-day cycle. Her last menstrual period began on 10 March. Using Naegele's rule, what is her expected date of delivery?
questions.e: Naegele's rule adds 1 year, subtracts 3 months and adds 7 days to the first day of the last menstrual period: 10 March gives 17 December. 10 December forgets to add the 7 days.

questions.s: Sana, 22, is 12 weeks pregnant. Her booking tests show HBsAg positive. She is otherwise well with normal liver enzymes. What is the most important measure to prevent transmission of hepatitis B to her baby?
o: Elective caesarean section at 38 to 39 weeks of gestation
Avoiding breastfeeding for the first six months
Interferon therapy during the second trimester
Vaccine and immunoglobulin to the newborn within 12 hours
questions.e: Birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine plus hepatitis B immunoglobulin given to the newborn within 12 hours greatly reduces vertical transmission. Caesarean section and avoiding breastfeeding do not add meaningful protection, and interferon is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman at 16 weeks of gestation has a raised fasting TSH and is started on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. Which physiological change in pregnancy most explains why women already on levothyroxine usually need a higher dose?
o: Increased thyroxine-binding globulin and placental deiodinase
Suppression of TSH by human placental lactogen
Decreased hepatic synthesis of binding proteins
questions.e: Oestrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, and the placenta metabolises T4 and the plasma volume expands, so the requirement for thyroxine rises by about a third. Renal iodine clearance actually increases in pregnancy, and it is hCG rather than placental lactogen that has a weak TSH-like effect.

questions.s: A primigravida at 20 weeks of gestation asks when tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine should be given in her pregnancy under the Pakistan EPI. She has never been vaccinated. What is the recommended schedule?
o: Two doses at least 4 weeks apart, the second at least 2 weeks before delivery
Three doses in the third trimester, one month apart
No vaccine in pregnancy; vaccinate after delivery
questions.e: An unimmunised pregnant woman needs two doses of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine at least 4 weeks apart, with the second given at least 2 weeks before delivery, to protect the newborn against neonatal tetanus. A single late dose does not give adequate protection.

questions.s: Bushra, 28, is 26 weeks pregnant and complains of burning on urination for two days. She has no fever or loin pain. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes. Which antibiotic is the most appropriate choice?
questions.e: Cefalexin is safe throughout pregnancy and effective for cystitis. Fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy, and trimethoprim is a folate antagonist best avoided in the first trimester while sulfonamides near term risk neonatal jaundice.

questions.s: A 29-year-old at 24 weeks of gestation has a symphysis-fundal height of 30 cm. Ultrasound shows a single fetus of appropriate size with a single deepest vertical pool of liquor of 11 cm. Which fetal anomaly is most likely to be associated?
questions.e: Polyhydramnios occurs when the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, as in oesophageal atresia or duodenal atresia. Renal agenesis and posterior urethral valves reduce fetal urine output and cause oligohydramnios, and pulmonary hypoplasia is a consequence of oligohydramnios.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman with epilepsy well controlled on sodium valproate plans to become pregnant in the next year. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue valproate and add folic acid 400 micrograms after conception
Stop all antiepileptic drugs once pregnancy is confirmed
Review with a neurologist to change to a safer drug and start high-dose folic acid before conception
questions.e: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm, so a specialist should switch to a safer agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception, with 5 mg folic acid. Stopping drugs abruptly in pregnancy risks status epilepticus, which is dangerous for mother and fetus.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman at 8 weeks of gestation presents with persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, a 6 % weight loss and ketonuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe vomiting in early pregnancy with more than 5 % weight loss, dehydration and ketonuria defines hyperemesis gravidarum. Gastroenteritis would usually include diarrhoea and a short course, and pyelonephritis would cause fever and loin pain.

questions.s: Fatima, 30, is 34 weeks pregnant and reports generalised itching, worse on her palms and soles, especially at night. There is no rash. Serum bile acids are raised and ALT is mildly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Itching of the palms and soles without a rash, with raised bile acids in the third trimester, is typical of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Polymorphic eruption has a visible urticarial rash, and acute fatty liver presents with vomiting, abdominal pain and liver failure.

questions.s: A primigravida at 30 weeks of gestation develops a vesicular rash. She has never had chickenpox. Two days earlier her nephew was diagnosed with varicella. She is afebrile and has no respiratory symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral aciclovir started within 24 hours of the rash
questions.e: A pregnant woman beyond 20 weeks who develops chickenpox should start oral aciclovir if she presents within 24 hours of the rash, to reduce maternal complications such as pneumonia. Immunoglobulin is post-exposure prophylaxis before a rash appears, and the live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation has a combined first-trimester screen. Which result pattern indicates an increased risk of trisomy 21?
o: Low free beta-hCG, low PAPP-A, normal nuchal translucency
Raised free beta-hCG, raised PAPP-A, reduced nuchal translucency
Raised free beta-hCG, low PAPP-A, increased nuchal translucency
Low free beta-hCG, raised PAPP-A, normal nuchal translucency
questions.e: In trisomy 21 the combined test typically shows raised free beta-hCG, low PAPP-A and increased nuchal translucency. Low beta-hCG with low PAPP-A suggests trisomy 18 or 13 instead.

questions.s: Nadia, 25, is 9 weeks pregnant and has had light vaginal bleeding and mild cramps. On speculum examination the cervical os is closed. Ultrasound shows a live intrauterine fetus with a heartbeat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bleeding with a closed os and a viable intrauterine pregnancy is a threatened miscarriage; most continue normally. An inevitable miscarriage has an open os, and a missed miscarriage shows a fetus without cardiac activity.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman presents to a THQ hospital with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea, left iliac fossa pain and slight vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable. Urine pregnancy test is positive. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
questions.e: In a stable woman with suspected ectopic pregnancy, transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line test to locate the pregnancy, combined with serial serum beta-hCG when needed. Laparoscopy is reserved for unstable patients or when imaging and hCG are inconclusive and treatment is needed.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with a tubal ectopic pregnancy is clinically stable with minimal pain. Ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm adnexal mass with no fetal heartbeat and no free fluid. Serum beta-hCG is 1,200 IU/L. Liver and renal function are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A small unruptured ectopic with no heartbeat, low beta-hCG and minimal pain in a stable woman who can attend follow-up is suitable for medical treatment with methotrexate. Surgery is preferred when beta-hCG is high, there is a fetal heartbeat, or there are signs of rupture.

questions.s: A 19-year-old at 11 weeks of gestation has vaginal bleeding and severe vomiting. The uterus is larger than dates. Serum beta-hCG is markedly raised. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous mass with multiple small cystic spaces and no fetus. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: This is a complete molar pregnancy, and suction evacuation is the treatment of choice, followed by serial hCG follow-up. Medical evacuation is avoided in complete moles because of the theoretical risk of embolising trophoblast, and hysterectomy is not first line in a young woman.

questions.s: Following evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, a 24-year-old woman is enrolled for follow-up. Which test is used to monitor her for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
questions.e: hCG is the tumour marker for trophoblastic disease; a plateau or rise after evacuation signals persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. CA-125 is a marker for epithelial ovarian cancer, and chest X-ray is used only for staging once neoplasia is diagnosed.

questions.s: Shazia, 31, gravida 3, is 34 weeks pregnant and presents with sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and non-tender and the fetal head is high. Fetal heart is normal. Which examination must be avoided until the diagnosis is clarified?
questions.e: Painless bleeding with a soft uterus and high presenting part suggests placenta praevia, and a digital vaginal examination can provoke torrential haemorrhage. Ultrasound should first localise the placenta; abdominal palpation is safe.

questions.s: Kiran, 27, is 36 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia. She develops sudden severe constant abdominal pain and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. The uterus is hard and tender, and the fetal heart rate is 90/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painful bleeding with a tense, woody, tender uterus and fetal distress in a woman with hypertension is typical of placental abruption; the visible bleeding often underestimates the concealed loss. Placenta praevia causes painless bleeding with a soft uterus.

questions.s: A 33-year-old in labour at term has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes. Immediately afterwards there is fresh vaginal bleeding and the fetal heart rate falls to a sinusoidal pattern then severe bradycardia. Maternal pulse and blood pressure are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bleeding at membrane rupture with rapid fetal compromise but a stable mother suggests vasa praevia: fetal vessels in the membranes tear and the blood lost is fetal. Abruption and uterine rupture typically cause maternal pain and haemodynamic change.

questions.s: A 27-year-old at 8 weeks of gestation has heavy bleeding with clots and cramping pain. Speculum examination shows an open os with products of conception in the canal. Her pulse is 120/min and blood pressure 85/50 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate step after starting resuscitation?
o: Remove the products from the os with sponge forceps
questions.e: Products of conception held in the cervical os cause vagal shock and bleeding; removing them with sponge forceps often rapidly improves the pulse and blood pressure. Delaying for imaging or medical treatment is inappropriate in a shocked patient.

questions.s: Saima, 36, has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. Which investigation is most appropriate for identifying a treatable cause?
questions.e: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage; aspirin with heparin improves live birth rates. TORCH screening has no role in recurrent miscarriage, and hysterosalpingography is not the first test for uterine anomalies in this setting.

questions.s: A 30-year-old with a previous caesarean section is 32 weeks pregnant. Ultrasound shows an anterior low-lying placenta covering the internal os over the scar, with loss of the retroplacental clear zone. What is the most likely complication at delivery?
o: Amniotic fluid embolism during the caesarean
Placenta accreta spectrum with massive haemorrhage
questions.e: Placenta praevia over a previous caesarean scar with loss of the clear zone strongly suggests placenta accreta spectrum, which carries a high risk of massive haemorrhage and hysterectomy. Delivery should be planned in a centre with blood bank and senior surgical support.

questions.s: A 26-year-old at 6 weeks of gestation with a pregnancy of unknown location has a beta-hCG of 900 IU/L. Forty-eight hours later it is 1,850 IU/L. She remains well. What does this pattern most suggest?
questions.e: A rise of more than about 63 % over 48 hours is consistent with a developing intrauterine pregnancy, which should be confirmed by ultrasound. A falling level suggests a failing pregnancy, and a suboptimal rise or plateau raises concern for an ectopic.

questions.s: Amna, 23, primigravida, is 32 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg on two readings 4 hours apart. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. She was normotensive at booking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New hypertension after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria defines pre-eclampsia. Gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or other organ involvement, and chronic hypertension is present before 20 weeks.

questions.s: A 25-year-old at 36 weeks of gestation with pre-eclampsia has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the labour ward. After securing the airway and placing her in the left lateral position, what is the drug of choice to control and prevent further seizures?
questions.e: Magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice for eclampsia; it is more effective than diazepam or phenytoin at preventing recurrent fits and reduces maternal death. Labetalol treats the blood pressure but does not prevent seizures.

questions.s: A woman receiving magnesium sulfate infusion for severe pre-eclampsia has a respiratory rate of 9/min, absent patellar reflexes and a urine output of 15 mL/hour. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the infusion and give intravenous calcium gluconate
Increase the infusion rate and give furosemide
Continue the infusion and start oxygen by mask
Give a bolus of intravenous diazepam
questions.e: Loss of reflexes and respiratory depression indicate magnesium toxicity, worsened by oliguria because magnesium is cleared by the kidneys. The infusion must be stopped and calcium gluconate given as the antidote. Furosemide and continuing the drug would be dangerous.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with chronic hypertension is 8 weeks pregnant. She takes enalapril. What is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive treatment?
o: Continue enalapril at the same dose
Stop treatment until the second trimester
questions.e: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are fetotoxic, causing renal damage and oligohydramnios, so they should be switched to a pregnancy-safe agent such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. Losartan carries the same risks as enalapril.

questions.s: Zainab, 38, gravida 4, has a history of severe pre-eclampsia in her last pregnancy. She is now 10 weeks pregnant. Which measure reduces her risk of pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy?
o: Low-dose aspirin daily from 12 weeks until delivery
Bed rest from 28 weeks of gestation
questions.e: Women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, including those with previous pre-eclampsia, should take low-dose aspirin daily from 12 weeks until birth. Salt restriction and bed rest have not been shown to prevent pre-eclampsia.

questions.s: A 28-year-old at 34 weeks of gestation with pre-eclampsia complains of epigastric pain and nausea. Hb is 9.2 g/dL with fragmented red cells on film, platelets 70 × 10⁹/L and ALT 310 U/L. Blood pressure is 160/105 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets in a woman with pre-eclampsia and epigastric pain is HELLP syndrome, and delivery is indicated after stabilisation. Acute fatty liver more often causes hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and renal failure, and hepatitis E does not explain the hypertension and haemolysis.

questions.s: A 26-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks has severe pre-eclampsia with blood pressure 170/112 mmHg. She has no headache or visual symptoms. Which drug is the most appropriate for urgent lowering of her blood pressure?
questions.e: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (160/110 mmHg or more) should be lowered promptly with intravenous labetalol, oral nifedipine or intravenous hydralazine. Captopril is an ACE inhibitor and diuretics reduce the already contracted plasma volume in pre-eclampsia.

questions.s: Which pathological process is considered central to the development of pre-eclampsia?
o: Inadequate trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries
Excessive placental production of placental growth factor
Reduced maternal sensitivity to angiotensin II
questions.e: In pre-eclampsia, trophoblast fails to invade and remodel the spiral arteries, leading to placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors that cause endothelial dysfunction. Placental growth factor is reduced, not raised, and sensitivity to angiotensin II is increased.

questions.s: Hira, 29, had an eclamptic fit 6 hours after a normal vaginal delivery and was treated with magnesium sulfate. For how long after the last seizure should the magnesium sulfate infusion usually be continued?
questions.e: Magnesium sulfate is continued for 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure, whichever is later, as the risk of further fits persists. Shorter courses increase the risk of recurrence.

questions.s: A 31-year-old at 29 weeks of gestation has gestational hypertension with blood pressure 145/95 mmHg, no proteinuria and normal blood tests. The fetus is well grown. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral labetalol with regular outpatient monitoring
Give corticosteroids and induce at 30 weeks
questions.e: Non-severe gestational hypertension is managed with an oral antihypertensive such as labetalol, targeting around 135/85 mmHg, with regular blood pressure, urine and fetal growth checks. Early delivery and magnesium sulfate are reserved for severe disease or pre-eclampsia with complications.

questions.s: Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in a pregnant woman with asthma?
questions.e: Labetalol is a non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-blocking activity and can provoke bronchospasm, so it should be avoided in asthma. Nifedipine is a suitable alternative for such women.

questions.s: A 34-year-old at 33 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia suddenly becomes breathless. Respiratory rate is 32/min, SpO₂ 86 % on air and there are bilateral fine crackles. She has received 3 litres of intravenous fluid over 12 hours. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Pre-eclampsia causes capillary leak and low oncotic pressure, so liberal intravenous fluids readily cause pulmonary oedema with bilateral crackles. Fluid restriction, usually around 80 mL/hour, prevents this; pulmonary embolism usually gives clear lungs on auscultation.

questions.s: Maryam, 27, at 28 weeks of gestation has severe early-onset pre-eclampsia, and delivery is being planned within the next 24 hours. Which additional drug should she receive before delivery for fetal benefit?
questions.e: Antenatal corticosteroids given before preterm birth reduce neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and death. Magnesium sulfate, which she will receive anyway, also gives fetal neuroprotection; tocolysis is inappropriate when delivery is indicated.

questions.s: Under WHO criteria, a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is done in a pregnant woman at 26 weeks. Which result alone is diagnostic of gestational diabetes?
questions.e: WHO thresholds for gestational diabetes are fasting 92 mg/dL or more, 1-hour 180 mg/dL or more, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL or more; any one value is enough. A fasting value of 95 mg/dL meets the criterion, while the other values are below threshold.

questions.s: Sadia, 32, has gestational diabetes diagnosed at 28 weeks. After two weeks of diet and exercise, her fasting glucose remains 110 mg/dL and 1-hour post-meal values are 160 to 175 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue diet and recheck in 4 weeks
Plan induction of labour at 34 weeks
questions.e: When diet and exercise fail to reach targets in gestational diabetes within one to two weeks, metformin is usually the first drug, with insulin added or substituted if targets are still not met. Pioglitazone is not used in pregnancy, and early delivery is not indicated for control alone.

questions.s: A baby born at 39 weeks to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes is jittery at 2 hours of age. Which neonatal complication is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Maternal hyperglycaemia causes fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which persists after birth when maternal glucose supply stops and causes early neonatal hypoglycaemia. Hypocalcaemia also occurs in infants of diabetic mothers but is less common and usually later.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman had gestational diabetes treated with diet in her pregnancy and delivered 6 weeks ago. Her blood glucose returned to normal after delivery. What follow-up is most appropriate?
o: Fasting glucose or HbA1c after delivery and then annually
Oral glucose tolerance test only if she becomes pregnant again
Lifelong metformin to prevent type 2 diabetes
questions.e: Women with previous gestational diabetes have a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes and should be tested after delivery and then annually. Lifelong metformin is not routinely recommended; lifestyle measures are the main prevention.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has an HbA1c of 10.5 % at 6 weeks of gestation. Which congenital anomaly is most specifically associated with poorly controlled pre-existing maternal diabetes?
questions.e: Caudal regression syndrome is rare but strongly associated with maternal pre-existing diabetes; congenital heart and neural tube defects are also more common. Gastroschisis is associated with young maternal age rather than diabetes.

questions.s: Which factor is the strongest indication to offer an oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks in a Pakistani woman attending antenatal clinic?
questions.e: A previous macrosomic baby of 4.5 kg or more is a recognised risk factor for gestational diabetes, along with obesity, previous gestational diabetes, family history and South Asian ethnicity. The other features are not risk factors.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is planning pregnancy. She takes metformin and her HbA1c is 8.9 %. What is the most appropriate preconception advice?
o: Conceive now and start insulin once pregnancy is confirmed
Folic acid 400 micrograms and conceive now
Stop metformin immediately before trying to conceive
Folic acid 5 mg and delay conception until HbA1c is below 6.5 %
questions.e: Women with diabetes should take high-dose folic acid (5 mg) and aim for an HbA1c below about 6.5 % before conceiving, as poor periconceptional control increases miscarriage and congenital anomalies. Metformin can be continued in pregnancy.

questions.s: A woman with insulin-treated gestational diabetes delivers a healthy baby. What should happen to her insulin immediately after delivery?
o: Continue the antenatal dose for 6 weeks
Halve the dose and continue for 2 weeks
Stop insulin and monitor capillary glucose
questions.e: Insulin resistance in gestational diabetes is driven by placental hormones, which fall rapidly after delivery, so glucose-lowering treatment is stopped and glucose is monitored to exclude persisting diabetes. Continuing antenatal doses risks hypoglycaemia.

questions.s: A 33-year-old at 36 weeks with gestational diabetes on insulin has an estimated fetal weight above the 97th centile on ultrasound. Which intrapartum complication is the baby at particular risk of?
questions.e: Macrosomia in diabetic pregnancy is associated with increased shoulder and trunk size relative to the head, so shoulder dystocia and brachial plexus injury are particular risks. The other complications are not specifically related to fetal size.

questions.s: Which placental hormone is chiefly responsible for the insulin resistance that develops in the second half of pregnancy?
questions.e: Human placental lactogen rises through pregnancy and antagonises insulin, diverting glucose to the fetus; progesterone, cortisol and prolactin contribute. hCG peaks in the first trimester and supports the corpus luteum rather than causing insulin resistance.

questions.s: A woman with gestational diabetes asks about target capillary glucose levels. Which fasting capillary glucose target is generally recommended?
questions.e: Most guidance aims for a fasting capillary glucose of about 95 mg/dL or less in pregnancy, with tight post-meal targets. A target of 126 mg/dL would allow fetal hyperinsulinaemia and macrosomia.

questions.s: A woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted at 30 weeks of gestation with vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul breathing. Capillary glucose is 220 mg/dL, blood ketones are high and venous pH is 7.18. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diabetic ketoacidosis occurs at lower glucose levels in pregnancy, and ketonaemia with acidosis confirms it despite glucose of only 220 mg/dL. It threatens the fetus and needs urgent treatment; hyperosmolar state involves very high glucose without significant ketosis.

questions.s: A primigravida is admitted in labour. On the partogram, cervical dilatation crosses the action line. What does this indicate?
o: Normal progress of the active phase
Slow progress needing assessment and intervention
questions.e: On the WHO partogram, crossing the alert line signals slow progress, and crossing the action line (4 hours to the right) means progress is abnormally slow and a decision on intervention is required. It is not a sign of normal or advanced labour.

questions.s: Parveen, 22, primigravida at term, has been fully dilated for 3 hours with an epidural. The head is at the ischial spines in occipito-posterior position with no caput. CTG is normal. Pelvis is adequate. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Wait a further 2 hours for spontaneous delivery
Assisted vaginal birth with rotation by a skilled operator
Emergency caesarean section without further assessment
Start oxytocin and encourage pushing for another hour
questions.e: Delay in the second stage in a nulliparous woman with an epidural, a head at the spines and a favourable assessment is managed with assisted vaginal birth, here requiring rotation. Waiting longer increases maternal and fetal risk, and caesarean is chosen if the assessment is unfavourable.

questions.s: A CTG in a woman in active labour at term shows a baseline of 140/min and variability of 10 beats. Decelerations begin with each contraction, mirror it and return to baseline as the contraction ends. What do these decelerations most likely reflect?
questions.e: Early decelerations mirror contractions and are caused by head compression, a vagal response that is benign. Late decelerations, which begin after the peak of the contraction, suggest uteroplacental insufficiency, and variable decelerations suggest cord compression.

questions.s: A multigravida at 38 weeks has spontaneous rupture of membranes. On vaginal examination, a loop of pulsating cord is felt in the vagina. Fetal heart rate is 90/min. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency caesarean
Push the cord back into the uterus and await labour
Start oxytocin infusion to speed delivery
Give terbutaline and repeat examination in 30 minutes
questions.e: In cord prolapse the presenting part should be elevated manually or by bladder filling, with the woman in knee-chest or left lateral position, while preparing for the quickest delivery, usually caesarean. Pushing the cord back is not recommended, and oxytocin would worsen compression.

questions.s: During delivery the fetal head is born but the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with gentle traction. Help has been called. What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?
o: Strong lateral traction on the head
questions.e: McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflexing the hips) with suprapubic pressure resolves most cases of shoulder dystocia. Fundal pressure and strong traction worsen impaction and cause brachial plexus injury.

questions.s: Shabana, 30, has a uterine contraction pattern of 5 in 10 minutes after starting oxytocin, and the CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 80/min for 4 minutes. She has had one previous caesarean section. Suddenly she reports severe constant pain, the presenting part has receded and contractions have stopped. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden pain, fetal bradycardia, loss of station of the presenting part and cessation of contractions in a woman with a uterine scar on oxytocin is uterine rupture. Abruption does not cause the presenting part to recede, and hyperstimulation alone would not stop contractions.

questions.s: A 27-year-old at 31 weeks of gestation presents with regular painful contractions. The cervix is 3 cm dilated and membranes are intact. Which intervention gives the greatest benefit to the newborn?
questions.e: Corticosteroids before preterm birth reduce neonatal death, respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular haemorrhage; magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is also given below about 32 weeks. Erythromycin is for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, not intact membranes, and progesterone has no role in established labour.

questions.s: A 25-year-old at 33 weeks has a gush of clear fluid per vagina. Speculum examination confirms pooling of liquor. She is afebrile, not contracting, and CTG is normal. What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?
o: No antibiotics unless she develops fever
questions.e: In preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, oral erythromycin for 10 days prolongs pregnancy and reduces neonatal morbidity. Co-amoxiclav is avoided because it is associated with necrotising enterocolitis in the newborn.

questions.s: Which Bishop score component is assessed by the position of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines?
questions.e: Station describes the level of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines; the Bishop score also includes dilatation, effacement or length, consistency and position of the cervix. A score of 8 or more indicates a favourable cervix for induction.

questions.s: A 29-year-old at 37 weeks has a breech presentation confirmed on ultrasound. She has no previous uterine surgery, the liquor volume is normal and the placenta is fundal. What should be offered first?
questions.e: External cephalic version should be offered to women with an uncomplicated breech at term, as it succeeds in about half and reduces caesarean rates. Caesarean or vaginal breech birth are considered if ECV fails or is declined.

questions.s: Rubina, 26, is in labour at term. Vaginal examination finds the anterior fontanelle and the supraorbital ridges at the os, and the presenting diameter is the mentovertical. What is the presentation?
questions.e: Brow presentation presents the mentovertical diameter, about 13.5 cm, which cannot pass through a normal pelvis, so caesarean is needed if it persists. Face presentation presents the submentobregmatic diameter and can deliver vaginally if mento-anterior.

questions.s: A multiparous woman at term has been in labour at a rural health centre for 30 hours. She is dehydrated, febrile and tachycardic. The bladder is distended, there is a Bandl's ring and the fetal head is 4/5 palpable with marked caput and moulding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged labour with a high head, severe moulding and caput, maternal exhaustion and a pathological retraction ring (Bandl's ring) indicates obstructed labour, which risks uterine rupture and fistula. Uterine inertia would not cause a retraction ring.

questions.s: Which of the following is the most important reason to avoid oxytocin augmentation in a multiparous woman with slow progress in labour?
o: Risk of uterine rupture from undiagnosed obstruction
Risk of water intoxication at low doses
questions.e: In multiparous women slow progress is more often due to obstruction or malposition, and oxytocin against an obstruction can rupture the uterus. Water intoxication occurs with high doses in large volumes of hypotonic fluid, not routine use.

questions.s: A CTG in labour shows a baseline of 160/min, reduced variability of 3 beats for 50 minutes and late decelerations with over half the contractions for 40 minutes. The cervix is 5 cm dilated. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue monitoring and reassess in 1 hour
Fetal blood sampling or expedited delivery
questions.e: Reduced variability with repeated late decelerations is a pathological trace suggesting fetal hypoxia, requiring correction of reversible causes and either fetal blood sampling or prompt delivery. Increasing oxytocin would worsen hypoxia.

questions.s: What is the normal duration of the third stage of labour with active management?
questions.e: With active management, the third stage is considered prolonged if the placenta is not delivered within 30 minutes; with physiological management the limit is 60 minutes. A retained placenta beyond this needs manual removal.

questions.s: Which drug is recommended by WHO as the first-choice uterotonic for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage at every birth?
questions.e: Oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly or intravenously after the birth of the baby is the recommended uterotonic for preventing PPH. Ergometrine is an alternative but is avoided in hypertension, and tranexamic acid is used in treatment of PPH rather than routine prevention.

questions.s: Noreen, 34, para 5, delivers a 4 kg baby. Ten minutes after delivery of a complete placenta she bleeds heavily. The uterus is soft and boggy and above the umbilicus. What is the most appropriate first step?
questions.e: A soft, enlarged uterus after delivery of a complete placenta indicates uterine atony, the commonest cause of PPH, treated first with fundal massage and uterotonics while resuscitation starts. Surgery is reserved for failure of medical and mechanical measures.

questions.s: A woman has a PPH of 1,200 mL from uterine atony despite oxytocin infusion and ergometrine. She is asthmatic. Which further uterotonic should be avoided?
questions.e: Carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha) causes bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analogue, is an acceptable alternative, and tranexamic acid should also be given within 3 hours of birth.

questions.s: A primigravida has a brisk bleed after a forceps delivery. The uterus is firm and well contracted and the placenta is complete. What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
questions.e: Continuing bleeding with a firm, contracted uterus after an instrumental delivery points to genital tract trauma, such as cervical, vaginal or perineal tears, which must be examined and repaired. Atony would cause a soft uterus.

questions.s: Immediately after delivery of the placenta with strong cord traction, a woman becomes shocked out of proportion to blood loss. The fundus cannot be felt abdominally and a mass is seen at the introitus. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Give ergometrine to contract the uterus
Remove the placenta and then pack the vagina
Immediate manual replacement of the uterus
questions.e: Uterine inversion causes vagal shock and haemorrhage and is treated by immediate manual replacement of the fundus, ideally with the placenta left attached if still adherent. Uterotonics before replacement would trap the inverted uterus.

questions.s: Within how many hours of birth should tranexamic acid be given to a woman with postpartum haemorrhage to reduce death from bleeding?
questions.e: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously reduces death from bleeding in PPH when given within 3 hours of birth; beyond this it shows no benefit. It should be given in addition to uterotonics, not instead of them.

questions.s: A woman bleeds heavily 10 days after a normal vaginal delivery. She has a temperature of 38.4 °C and a tender uterus with an open os. What is the most likely cause?
o: Retained products of conception with infection
questions.e: Secondary PPH (24 hours to 12 weeks after birth) is most often due to retained products and endometritis, suggested here by fever and a tender, open uterus. Atony is a cause of primary PPH within 24 hours.

questions.s: A woman with PPH from atony continues to bleed despite uterotonics and bimanual compression. She is in a THQ hospital awaiting transfer for surgery. Which measure is most appropriate as a temporising step?
questions.e: Intrauterine balloon tamponade (including a condom catheter) is an effective temporising measure for atonic PPH refractory to drugs. Vaginal packing does not compress the uterine cavity and conceals bleeding.

questions.s: What volume of blood loss after a vaginal delivery is the usual definition of primary postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.e: Primary PPH is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth, and major PPH is over 1,000 mL. Blood loss is often underestimated, so clinical signs matter.

questions.s: A woman with severe abruption and a dead fetus starts to bleed from venepuncture sites. Platelets are 50 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is markedly raised. What is the underlying process?
questions.e: Placental abruption releases tissue factor into the maternal circulation, triggering DIC with consumption of platelets and fibrinogen and high fibrin degradation products. Treatment is delivery with replacement of blood products; ITP does not cause low fibrinogen.

questions.s: Five days after a caesarean section, Asma, 28, has fever of 39 °C, lower abdominal pain and foul-smelling lochia. The uterus is tender and subinvoluted. Pulse is 118/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, uterine tenderness, subinvolution and offensive lochia after delivery indicate endometritis, the commonest cause of puerperal sepsis, particularly after caesarean section. It needs broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics; pyelonephritis would cause loin pain and urinary symptoms.

questions.s: A breastfeeding mother 3 weeks after delivery has a painful, red, wedge-shaped area on the right breast with fever of 38.2 °C. There is no fluctuant mass. What is the most appropriate advice about breastfeeding?
o: Stop breastfeeding from both breasts until recovery
Feed only from the left breast and discard right milk
Express and discard milk while on antibiotics
questions.e: In lactational mastitis effective milk removal is central to treatment, so breastfeeding should continue from both breasts, with flucloxacillin if symptoms persist or she is unwell. Stopping feeding causes milk stasis and increases the risk of abscess.

questions.s: On the third day after delivery a mother is tearful, irritable and anxious, but sleeps when the baby sleeps, cares for the baby well and has no thoughts of harm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Postnatal blues are common, start around day 3 to 5 and resolve within 2 weeks with reassurance and support. Postnatal depression lasts longer than 2 weeks with persistent low mood and loss of function.

questions.s: Ten days after delivery a 24-year-old woman with a family history of bipolar disorder becomes confused, sleepless and agitated, and believes her baby has been replaced. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start an SSRI in primary care
Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally to a mother and baby unit
questions.e: Puerperal psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with risk to mother and baby and needs urgent specialist assessment and admission. Bipolar disorder in the woman or a first-degree relative is a strong risk factor; outpatient SSRI treatment is inadequate.

questions.s: Two weeks after caesarean section, Farzana, 36, with a BMI of 34, develops a painful swollen left calf. Compression ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. She is breastfeeding. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Low-molecular-weight heparin is the standard treatment for postpartum venous thromboembolism and is safe with breastfeeding; warfarin can be used later. Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended while breastfeeding because of limited safety data.

questions.s: A woman who delivered 6 days ago asks when her uterus should no longer be palpable abdominally. When does the uterus normally become a pelvic organ after childbirth?
questions.e: After delivery the fundus is at the umbilicus and descends about 1 cm a day, so it is usually no longer palpable abdominally by about 10 to 14 days. By 6 weeks it has returned to near its non-pregnant size.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman wishes to start contraception 4 weeks after delivery. She is exclusively breastfeeding. Which method should be avoided at this time?
questions.e: Combined hormonal contraception is avoided in breastfeeding women before 6 weeks postpartum because it reduces milk supply and raises venous thromboembolism risk. Progestogen-only methods and the copper IUD are suitable.

questions.s: Shagufta, 24, is 28 weeks pregnant. Hb is 8.6 g/dL, MCV 70 fL and serum ferritin 8 micrograms/L. She is well with no symptoms. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
questions.e: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy is treated first with oral iron, with a repeat Hb after 2 to 3 weeks to confirm response; intravenous iron is used if oral iron fails or is not tolerated, or close to term. Transfusion is reserved for severe or symptomatic anaemia near delivery or bleeding.

questions.s: A 22-year-old at 14 weeks of gestation has Hb 10.2 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, normal ferritin and red cell count of 6.1 × 10¹²/L. Her husband is her first cousin. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Marked microcytosis with a high red cell count and normal ferritin suggests beta thalassaemia trait, which should be confirmed with HbA2 measurement by HPLC or electrophoresis. Her husband should then be tested, as both being carriers gives a 1 in 4 risk of thalassaemia major.

questions.s: If both parents are confirmed carriers of beta thalassaemia trait, what is the risk in each pregnancy that the child will have beta thalassaemia major?
questions.e: Beta thalassaemia is autosomal recessive, so two carrier parents have a 25 % chance of an affected child, 50 % of a carrier and 25 % of an unaffected child in each pregnancy. This is the basis for prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with twins at 26 weeks has Hb 9.5 g/dL with MCV 108 fL. She takes phenytoin for epilepsy and did not take supplements. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e: Multiple pregnancy increases folate requirement, and phenytoin interferes with folate absorption, causing macrocytic anaemia. Vitamin B12 deficiency is less likely without dietary restriction or malabsorption.

questions.s: Which haemoglobin level defines anaemia in pregnancy according to WHO?
questions.e: WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as Hb below 11 g/dL. The cut-off of 12 g/dL applies to non-pregnant women; the lower threshold in pregnancy reflects physiological haemodilution.

questions.s: Which physiological change explains the mild fall in haemoglobin concentration seen in a healthy pregnancy?
o: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
Increased red cell destruction by the spleen
Reduced iron absorption from the gut
questions.e: Plasma volume increases by about 50 % but red cell mass by only about 25 %, causing a physiological dilutional fall in Hb. Iron absorption actually increases in pregnancy, and erythropoietin rises.

questions.s: A woman at 36 weeks with Hb 7.1 g/dL due to iron deficiency is mildly breathless on exertion. She cannot tolerate oral iron. Delivery is expected within 4 weeks. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Switch to a different oral iron salt
questions.e: Late in pregnancy, or when oral iron is not tolerated, parenteral iron raises Hb faster and more reliably than another oral preparation, helping prepare her for delivery. Erythropoietin is not a routine treatment for iron deficiency in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 28-year-old with sickle cell disease is 20 weeks pregnant. Which complication is she at particular risk of during pregnancy?
questions.e: Pregnancy in sickle cell disease increases the frequency of painful crises, acute chest syndrome, infection, pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction, so care is shared with a haematologist and low-dose aspirin is advised. It is not associated with gestational diabetes or polyhydramnios.

questions.s: A 23-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks is found to be rubella non-immune at booking. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Give MMR vaccine at this visit
questions.e: MMR is a live vaccine and is avoided in pregnancy, so non-immune women are vaccinated after delivery and advised to avoid contact with rash illness meanwhile. Immunoglobulin is not given routinely to non-exposed women.

questions.s: At what gestation is the routine fetal anomaly ultrasound scan usually performed?
questions.e: The detailed anomaly scan is done at about 18 to 21 weeks, when fetal structures can be examined well and options remain if a major anomaly is found. The 11 to 14 week scan is for dating and nuchal translucency.

questions.s: Lubna, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant and reports that her baby has moved much less over the past day. She has no pain or bleeding. Fetal heart is heard with a handheld Doppler. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and ask her to count kicks at home
questions.e: Reduced fetal movements after 28 weeks warrant a CTG to assess fetal wellbeing, with ultrasound if growth restriction or other risk factors are suspected. Hearing the heart once does not exclude fetal compromise, and simple reassurance misses at-risk babies.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman at 16 weeks has a reactive treponemal test and an RPR titre of 1:32 on booking screening. She has no penicillin allergy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral azithromycin as a single dose
questions.e: Penicillin is the only treatment reliably preventing congenital syphilis, and benzathine penicillin is used in pregnancy. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, and delaying treatment allows fetal infection.

questions.s: A woman at 36 weeks feels faint and nauseated when lying flat on her back for an ultrasound. Her blood pressure drops to 85/50 mmHg. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tilt her to the left lateral position
Sit her upright with the head of the bed at 90°
questions.e: Supine hypotension is caused by the gravid uterus compressing the inferior vena cava and reducing venous return; left lateral tilt relieves it. Sitting upright alone does not relieve aortocaval compression as reliably.

questions.s: Rehana, 29, has an uncomplicated pregnancy dated by early ultrasound. She is now 41 weeks and has not gone into labour. What should she be offered?
questions.e: Induction of labour is offered from about 41 weeks in uncomplicated pregnancies to reduce stillbirth and perinatal death. Caesarean section is not indicated for prolonged pregnancy alone.

questions.s: A 31-year-old at 32 weeks has an ultrasound estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile with reduced liquor. What is the most useful investigation to assess fetal wellbeing and guide timing of delivery?
questions.e: In a small-for-gestational-age fetus, umbilical artery Doppler is the key surveillance test; absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates placental insufficiency and influences delivery timing. Biometry repeated after 4 weeks is too slow for a severely growth-restricted fetus.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed HIV-positive at her booking visit at 14 weeks. Her CD4 count is 650 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate management to prevent mother-to-child transmission?
o: Start antiretroviral therapy now and continue for life
Start ART only if CD4 falls below 350
Give zidovudine to the baby only after birth
Delay ART until 28 weeks of gestation
questions.e: WHO recommends lifelong antiretroviral therapy for all pregnant women with HIV regardless of CD4 count, started as soon as possible; suppression of viral load is the main way to prevent transmission. Delaying treatment increases the risk of in-utero transmission.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman on long-term warfarin after a previous pulmonary embolism finds she is 5 weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate change to her anticoagulation?
o: Stop anticoagulation until the third trimester
questions.e: Warfarin is teratogenic between about 6 and 12 weeks (warfarin embryopathy), so she should change to low-molecular-weight heparin before then. Direct oral anticoagulants are not used in pregnancy, and stopping anticoagulation risks recurrent thrombosis.

questions.s: A woman at 30 weeks of gestation has a serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. Her non-pregnant value was 0.8 mg/dL. Why might this result be of concern?
o: Creatinine is not affected by pregnancy
GFR rises in pregnancy, so creatinine is normally lower
Creatinine values only matter after delivery
questions.e: Renal blood flow and GFR rise by about 50 % in pregnancy, so serum creatinine normally falls; a value at the upper end of the non-pregnant range may indicate renal impairment. This is relevant when assessing pre-eclampsia.

questions.s: Saba, 29, had a scan at 7 weeks showing a live intrauterine pregnancy. At 9 weeks she had heavy bleeding with clots which has now settled. The os is closed and ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a thin endometrium. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Bleeding that has settled with a closed os and an empty uterus, after a previously confirmed intrauterine pregnancy, is a complete miscarriage. Without the earlier confirmed intrauterine pregnancy, an ectopic would need to be excluded.

questions.s: A 33-year-old at 10 weeks by dates has a dating scan without any symptoms. Ultrasound shows an intrauterine fetus with a crown-rump length of 9 mm and no cardiac activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A crown-rump length of 7 mm or more with no heartbeat confirms a non-viable pregnancy; without bleeding or passage of tissue this is a missed (silent) miscarriage. Threatened miscarriage requires a viable fetus.

questions.s: A 24-year-old with 6 weeks of amenorrhoea collapses with severe abdominal pain and shoulder-tip pain. Pulse is 130/min, BP 80/40 mmHg and the abdomen is distended and tender. Pregnancy test is positive. After resuscitation is started, what is the definitive management?
questions.e: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemodynamic instability needs immediate surgery, usually salpingectomy, alongside resuscitation. Methotrexate and serial hCG are only for stable women with unruptured ectopics.

questions.s: What is the most common site of an ectopic pregnancy?
questions.e: About 70 to 80 % of ectopic pregnancies implant in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. Isthmic ectopics are less common but rupture earlier because the isthmus is narrow.

questions.s: Which factor in a woman's history most increases her risk of an ectopic pregnancy?
o: Use of the combined oral contraceptive pill
questions.e: Pelvic inflammatory disease damages tubal cilia and causes adhesions, a major risk factor for ectopic pregnancy, as are previous ectopic and tubal surgery. The combined pill suppresses ovulation and reduces ectopic risk.

questions.s: Three days after an unsafe abortion by an untrained provider, a 30-year-old woman presents with fever of 39.5 °C, offensive vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain and a tender, bulky uterus. Pulse is 120/min. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral antibiotics and outpatient review in 48 hours
questions.e: Septic abortion requires resuscitation, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and prompt evacuation of infected retained products, which are the source of sepsis. Hysterectomy is reserved for uterine perforation with severe sepsis or failure to respond.

questions.s: A 26-year-old Rh-negative woman with no anti-D antibodies has a surgical evacuation for a missed miscarriage at 11 weeks. What is the most appropriate step regarding anti-D?
o: No anti-D is needed before 20 weeks
Check the father's blood group first and give anti-D only if he is Rh-positive
Give anti-D at 28 weeks of her next pregnancy
questions.e: Anti-D should be given within 72 hours to Rh-negative non-sensitised women after surgical management of miscarriage, as well as after ectopic pregnancy, to prevent sensitisation. Waiting until the next pregnancy is too late.

questions.s: Which karyotype is typical of a partial hydatidiform mole?
questions.e: A partial mole is usually triploid, with one maternal and two paternal haploid sets, and may contain fetal parts. A complete mole is diploid, usually 46,XX, with all chromosomes paternal and no fetal tissue.

questions.s: At the 20-week anomaly scan, Mehwish's placenta is reported as low-lying, reaching the internal os. She has had no bleeding. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Book an elective caesarean section at 37 weeks
Admit for bed rest until delivery
questions.e: Most placentas that are low-lying at 20 weeks move away from the os as the lower segment forms, so a repeat scan at about 32 weeks confirms the final position. She should be advised to attend if bleeding occurs; admission is not needed if asymptomatic.

questions.s: Which blood pressure reading defines severe hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.e: Severe hypertension in pregnancy is a systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or more or a diastolic of 110 mmHg or more and needs prompt treatment to prevent stroke. Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as 140/90 mmHg or more.

questions.s: Four days after a normal delivery, Tahira, 26, presents with severe frontal headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 165/110 mmHg and urine shows 2+ protein. Her antenatal blood pressures were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pre-eclampsia can present for the first time after delivery, typically within the first week, with hypertension, proteinuria and headache; magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives are needed. Post-dural puncture headache is postural and not associated with hypertension or proteinuria.

questions.s: A woman receiving magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia is being monitored on the labour ward. Which clinical sign is the earliest useful indicator of magnesium toxicity?
questions.e: Loss of deep tendon reflexes occurs before respiratory depression and cardiac arrest, so patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output are checked regularly. Magnesium causes hypotension and bradycardia rather than hypertension or tachycardia.

questions.s: Which fetal complication is most commonly associated with early-onset pre-eclampsia?
questions.e: Placental insufficiency in pre-eclampsia causes fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios, so fetal growth and Doppler are monitored. Macrosomia and polyhydramnios are features of diabetic pregnancy.

questions.s: A 28-year-old primigravida with pre-eclampsia that is well controlled on oral labetalol reaches 37 weeks. Blood tests and fetal monitoring are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Delivery is recommended for women with pre-eclampsia from 37 weeks, as continuing the pregnancy carries maternal risk without fetal benefit. Expectant management is used before 37 weeks when the mother and fetus are stable.

questions.s: Which of the following places a woman at high risk of pre-eclampsia, so that low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks is recommended?
o: Second pregnancy with the same partner
questions.e: Autoimmune disease such as SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, along with chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes and previous hypertensive disease in pregnancy. A second pregnancy with the same partner lowers rather than raises the risk.

questions.s: Nazia, 30, took methyldopa for gestational hypertension and delivered 2 days ago. Her blood pressure still needs treatment. Why is methyldopa usually changed to another antihypertensive after delivery?
o: It is secreted in large amounts in breast milk
It increases the risk of postnatal depression
questions.e: Methyldopa is associated with depression, so it is stopped within days of delivery and replaced, for example with enalapril, nifedipine or labetalol, all compatible with breastfeeding. Its passage into breast milk is small.

questions.s: At a BHU, a 20-year-old at 35 weeks has an eclamptic fit. She is now post-ictal, lying on her left side with a clear airway. BP is 170/110 mmHg. The nearest hospital is two hours away. What is the most appropriate action before transfer?
o: Give the loading dose of magnesium sulfate and refer urgently
Give intravenous diazepam and transfer without further treatment
Start oxytocin to deliver at the BHU
Wait at the BHU until the blood pressure settles
questions.e: Where full care is not available, the loading dose of magnesium sulfate (intramuscular if needed) should be given before urgent referral, as it is the most effective way to prevent further fits. Diazepam is inferior, and delaying transfer or attempting delivery at the BHU is unsafe.

questions.s: A woman at 30 weeks has new hypertension and 1+ protein on urine dipstick. Which test best quantifies her proteinuria?
questions.e: A urine protein:creatinine ratio of 30 mg/mmol or more, or an albumin:creatinine ratio, confirms significant proteinuria quickly and replaces most 24-hour collections. Serum albumin does not measure urinary protein loss.

questions.s: Tasneem, 31, had gestational diabetes in her last pregnancy and is now 9 weeks pregnant. Her booking random glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate screening plan for diabetes in this pregnancy?
o: Early testing as soon as possible, then OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks if normal
questions.e: Women with previous gestational diabetes should be tested early in pregnancy, by OGTT or self-monitoring, and again at 24 to 28 weeks if the first test is normal, because recurrence is common. Glycosuria is an unreliable screening test in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes has an uncomplicated pregnancy with good glucose control and normal fetal growth. When should elective birth usually be planned?
questions.e: Women with pre-existing diabetes are offered planned birth between 37+0 and 38+6 weeks because of the higher risk of late stillbirth. Earlier delivery is considered only for maternal or fetal complications.

questions.s: A woman with insulin-treated diabetes is in established labour. Within which capillary blood glucose range should her glucose be kept during labour?
questions.e: Capillary glucose is kept at about 4 to 7 mmol/L (72 to 126 mg/dL) during labour, usually with an intravenous insulin and dextrose infusion, to reduce neonatal hypoglycaemia. Higher maternal glucose increases fetal insulin secretion at birth.

questions.s: A baby born at 38 weeks to a mother with poorly controlled diabetes develops tachypnoea and grunting with a ground-glass chest X-ray. What is the mechanism of this baby's respiratory problem?
questions.e: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia antagonises cortisol and delays lung maturation and surfactant synthesis, so infants of diabetic mothers can have respiratory distress syndrome even near term. Diabetes causes polyhydramnios, not oligohydramnios.

questions.s: Which test is used to diagnose gestational diabetes in a woman at 26 weeks of gestation?
questions.e: Gestational diabetes is diagnosed with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, usually at 24 to 28 weeks. HbA1c falls in normal pregnancy and is not sensitive enough to diagnose gestational diabetes.

questions.s: Sumaira, 24, at 22 weeks has 1+ glycosuria on a routine dipstick. Her random plasma glucose is 96 mg/dL. Why is glycosuria common in normal pregnancy?
o: Increased GFR exceeds tubular glucose reabsorption
Placental lactogen raises the renal threshold
Oestrogen blocks renal glucose transporters completely
questions.e: Rising GFR increases the filtered load of glucose beyond the reabsorptive capacity of the tubules, so glycosuria is common and unreliable as a screening test. A formal OGTT is needed if there are risk factors.

questions.s: A 33-year-old with type 2 diabetes for 8 years books at 8 weeks of gestation. Which assessment should be arranged at booking because pregnancy can cause rapid progression of a diabetic complication?
questions.e: Diabetic retinopathy can progress rapidly in pregnancy, especially with sudden tightening of control, so retinal assessment is done at booking and repeated later. The other tests are not routinely needed in pregnancy.

questions.s: A healthy term baby is born to a mother with gestational diabetes on insulin. What is the most appropriate first step to prevent neonatal hypoglycaemia?
o: Admission to the neonatal unit for observation
Early breastfeeding within the first hour
questions.e: Babies of diabetic mothers should feed as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 30 minutes to an hour, with blood glucose checked before the second feed. Routine neonatal unit admission and intravenous dextrose are needed only if hypoglycaemia occurs or the baby is unwell.

questions.s: A woman with poorly controlled gestational diabetes has polyhydramnios at 32 weeks. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Fetal hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis and fetal polyuria, increasing amniotic fluid volume. Swallowing disorders also cause polyhydramnios but are not related to maternal diabetes.

questions.s: On abdominal examination of a primigravida at 38 weeks, two-fifths of the fetal head is palpable above the pelvic brim. What does this indicate?
o: The head is free and not engaged
The fetus is in breech presentation
questions.e: When two-fifths or less of the head is palpable abdominally, the widest diameter has passed the pelvic brim, meaning the head is engaged. Three-fifths or more palpable means the head is not engaged.

questions.s: During a normal vaginal delivery in occipito-anterior position, the head has just been born by extension. Which movement follows next?
questions.e: After the head is born by extension it rotates back to realign with the shoulders (restitution), followed by external rotation as the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter. Flexion and internal rotation occur earlier in labour.

questions.s: In a well-flexed vertex presentation, which fetal skull diameter presents to the pelvis?
questions.e: Full flexion presents the suboccipitobregmatic diameter, the smallest, which favours normal delivery. The occipitofrontal diameter presents with deflexion, as in occipito-posterior positions, and submentobregmatic with face presentation.

questions.s: What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate at term on a CTG?
questions.e: A normal baseline fetal heart rate at term is 110 to 160 beats per minute with variability of 5 to 25 beats. Persistent tachycardia may indicate maternal fever, infection or hypoxia.

questions.s: After rupture of membranes, a CTG shows decelerations of varying shape, depth and timing in relation to contractions, with rapid falls and recoveries. Variability is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Variable decelerations are the commonest type in labour and reflect umbilical cord compression, often after membrane rupture when liquor volume falls. Late decelerations, with a uniform shape starting after the contraction peak, reflect uteroplacental insufficiency.

questions.s: Labour is to be induced in a 28-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks with intact membranes. Her Bishop score is 3. What is the most appropriate first method?
questions.e: With an unfavourable cervix (Bishop score below about 6) cervical ripening with a vaginal prostaglandin or a balloon catheter comes first. Amniotomy and oxytocin are used once the cervix is favourable.

questions.s: Ten minutes after an epidural is sited in labour, a woman feels dizzy and her blood pressure falls from 120/75 to 85/50 mmHg. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Regional anaesthesia blocks sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilatation and hypotension, which is treated with left lateral tilt, fluids and a vasopressor. Total spinal anaesthesia causes rapid ascending block with respiratory difficulty and loss of consciousness.

questions.s: After a vaginal delivery, examination shows a perineal tear involving the external anal sphincter and the internal anal sphincter, with intact rectal mucosa. How is this tear classified?
questions.e: Third-degree tears involve the anal sphincter complex: 3a less than half of the external sphincter, 3b more than half, and 3c includes the internal sphincter. A fourth-degree tear also involves the anorectal mucosa.

questions.s: A 26-year-old has a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. At 20 weeks one twin has polyhydramnios with a distended bladder and the other has severe oligohydramnios with a non-visible bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome results from unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic twins, giving a polyuric, polyhydramniotic recipient and an oliguric donor. It is treated with fetoscopic laser ablation in specialist centres.

questions.s: A 23-year-old at 30 weeks of gestation is in threatened preterm labour with intact membranes. Corticosteroids are being given. Which drug is commonly used as a tocolytic to delay delivery for 48 hours?
questions.e: Nifedipine is widely used as a tocolytic to delay birth long enough to complete steroids and allow transfer, with fewer side effects than beta-agonists. Prolonged indometacin risks premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios.

questions.s: Which antenatal factor most increases the risk of atonic postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.e: Overdistension of the uterus by multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios or macrosomia predisposes to atony; grand multiparity, prolonged labour and chorioamnionitis also raise the risk. Blood group and a previous normal delivery do not.

questions.s: A woman with pre-eclampsia has heavy bleeding after delivery from uterine atony. Which uterotonic should be avoided?
questions.e: Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and can provoke severe hypertension and stroke, so it is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Oxytocin, misoprostol and carboprost (if not asthmatic) remain options.

questions.s: Forty-five minutes after an actively managed vaginal delivery, the placenta has not been delivered despite controlled cord traction. Blood loss is 250 mL and she is stable. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Intramuscular ergometrine and strong cord traction
Fundal pressure to expel the placenta
Manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia
questions.e: A placenta retained beyond 30 minutes with active management needs manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia, with antibiotic cover. Excessive cord traction or fundal pressure risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion.

questions.s: Six weeks after a massive postpartum haemorrhage requiring transfusion of 8 units, Shamim, 32, has been unable to breastfeed, feels tired and cold, and has not resumed menstruation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe hypotension from PPH can cause ischaemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary in pregnancy, presenting with failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and features of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea but not lactation failure or hypothyroid features.

questions.s: Which of the following is a component of active management of the third stage of labour?
o: Controlled cord traction after a uterotonic
Fundal pressure to expel the placenta
Waiting for the placenta to deliver by maternal effort
questions.e: Active management includes a uterotonic after birth, controlled cord traction by a skilled attendant and checking uterine tone. Delayed cord clamping of 1 to 3 minutes is now recommended, and fundal pressure is avoided.

questions.s: During a caesarean section, the uterus remains atonic and bleeding continues despite oxytocin, ergometrine and carboprost. The woman wishes to keep her fertility. What is the purpose of a B-Lynch suture in this situation?
o: To tie the internal iliac arteries
To compress the atonic uterus mechanically
To close the placental bed vessels individually
questions.e: The B-Lynch brace suture compresses the uterus vertically, controlling atonic bleeding while preserving the uterus. Internal iliac artery ligation and hysterectomy are other surgical options if it fails.

questions.s: A lady health worker attends a home birth in a remote village where oxytocin is not available. Which drug is recommended to prevent postpartum haemorrhage in this setting?
questions.e: Where oxytocin cannot be stored or given, WHO supports oral misoprostol for PPH prevention, including by trained community health workers. Ergometrine requires cold storage and an injection and is contraindicated in hypertension.

questions.s: What is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.e: Uterine atony (tone) causes most cases of primary PPH, followed by trauma, tissue and thrombin (the 4 Ts). Assessment always starts by checking whether the uterus is contracted.

questions.s: A 35-year-old in strong labour after amniotomy suddenly becomes breathless and cyanosed, then collapses with hypotension. Shortly afterwards she bleeds from cannula sites and the vagina. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden cardiorespiratory collapse in labour or soon after delivery followed by DIC is typical of amniotic fluid embolism, a rare obstetric emergency with high mortality. Eclampsia presents with seizures and hypertension rather than collapse with early coagulopathy.

questions.s: A first-time mother asks what vaginal discharge to expect after childbirth. Which description is normal?
o: Red for 3 to 4 days, then pinkish-brown, then yellowish-white for up to about 6 weeks
Clear and watery from the first day, stopping within one week
Red and heavy throughout for 6 weeks
No discharge after the first 24 hours
questions.e: Lochia is red (rubra) for the first few days, then pink-brown (serosa) and then yellowish-white (alba), lasting up to about 6 weeks. Persistent heavy red lochia or offensive lochia suggests retained products or infection.

questions.s: Which tool is commonly used to screen mothers for postnatal depression?
questions.e: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item questionnaire validated for postnatal depression screening, including in Urdu. The MMSE assesses cognition and CAGE screens for alcohol misuse.

questions.s: On day 3 after delivery, a mother has both breasts swollen, firm and tender, with a temperature of 37.6 °C. There is no localised redness. The baby is feeding infrequently. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop breastfeeding and bind the breasts
Frequent feeding on demand with good attachment
questions.e: Bilateral swelling and tenderness around day 3 is breast engorgement, relieved by frequent effective feeding or expression. Antibiotics are for mastitis with localised inflammation and systemic upset, and drainage for abscess.

questions.s: Ruqaiya, 25, delivered 3 months ago. She is exclusively breastfeeding day and night and her periods have not returned. She asks whether breastfeeding protects her from pregnancy. What is the correct advice?
o: She is protected only until 6 weeks after delivery
Protection continues until she stops breastfeeding entirely
The lactational amenorrhoea method is highly effective while these conditions last up to 6 months
questions.e: The lactational amenorrhoea method is over 98 % effective if the woman is fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic and less than 6 months postpartum. Once any condition is not met she needs another method.

questions.s: Eight hours after a vaginal delivery with an epidural, a woman has not passed urine. She has lower abdominal discomfort and a palpable bladder. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Encourage oral fluids and wait 12 hours
questions.e: Postpartum urinary retention is common after epidural and instrumental delivery and should be managed promptly by catheterisation to prevent bladder overdistension and long-term dysfunction. Furosemide would worsen distension.

questions.s: A pregnant woman starting oral iron asks how to take it to improve absorption. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Take it with tea or milk
Take it with a source of vitamin C such as orange juice
Take it together with calcium tablets
questions.e: Vitamin C enhances absorption of non-haem iron, while tea, milk, calcium and antacids reduce it. Iron is best taken on an empty stomach or with orange juice, separate from calcium supplements.

questions.s: A 22-year-old at 20 weeks of gestation from a rural area of Punjab, where she works barefoot in fields, has iron deficiency anaemia with Hb 8.9 g/dL and eosinophilia. Which additional treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Hookworm infection is a common cause of iron deficiency in rural areas, suggested by barefoot field work and eosinophilia; WHO supports deworming with albendazole after the first trimester in endemic areas, along with iron. Praziquantel treats schistosomiasis and tapeworms.

questions.s: Which outcome is most associated with severe maternal anaemia in pregnancy?
o: Low birth weight and preterm birth
questions.e: Severe maternal anaemia is associated with low birth weight, preterm birth, perinatal death and poor maternal tolerance of haemorrhage. It is not associated with macrosomia or post-term pregnancy.

questions.s: A pregnant woman with iron deficiency anaemia starts oral iron. What is the earliest laboratory sign of response to treatment?
o: Rise in serum ferritin within 2 days
Rise in reticulocyte count within about 7 to 10 days
Rise in Hb of 4 g/dL within 1 week
questions.e: A reticulocyte response peaks about 7 to 10 days after starting effective iron, followed by a rise in Hb over the next weeks. MCV normalises slowly, and ferritin reflects stores, which fill last.

questions.s: Mehreen, 16, has never menstruated. She has normal breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. The vagina is a short blind pouch and ultrasound shows no uterus with normal ovaries. Karyotype is 46,XX. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics, a 46,XX karyotype and absent uterus is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome; ovarian function is normal. Androgen insensitivity also gives a blind vagina and absent uterus, but with a 46,XY karyotype and scanty pubic and axillary hair.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman has had no periods since a repeat dilatation and curettage for secondary postpartum haemorrhage with endometritis 8 months ago. Pregnancy test is negative. FSH, LH, prolactin and TSH are normal. She has no bleeding after a progestogen and then an oestrogen-progestogen challenge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Intrauterine adhesions after curettage of a recently pregnant or infected uterus cause Asherman syndrome; failure to bleed even after oestrogen and progestogen with normal hormones points to an endometrial cause. Premature ovarian insufficiency would show raised FSH.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman has 6 months of amenorrhoea and milky nipple discharge. She takes no medication and pregnancy test is negative. Serum prolactin is markedly raised, TSH is normal and MRI shows a 6 mm pituitary adenoma. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline are first-line for prolactinomas, lowering prolactin, shrinking the tumour and restoring ovulation. Surgery is reserved for intolerance or resistance to medical treatment.

questions.s: Hina, 17, has painful periods since menarche at 13. The pain starts with the onset of bleeding, lasts 2 days and is cramping in the lower abdomen. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: NSAID started at the onset of pain
questions.e: Pain starting with menstruation in a young woman with a normal examination suggests primary dysmenorrhoea, caused by prostaglandins, so NSAIDs are first line, with the combined pill as an alternative. Laparoscopy is considered only if symptoms fail to respond or secondary causes are suspected.

questions.s: A 31-year-old woman has worsening dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and 3 years of infertility. Pelvic examination shows a fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodules in the posterior fornix. Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: The features suggest endometriosis, and laparoscopy with histological confirmation is the gold standard for diagnosis. Ultrasound can identify endometriomas and deep nodules but may miss superficial peritoneal disease, and CA-125 is non-specific.

questions.s: Zubaida, 58, presents with vaginal bleeding two years after her last period. She is not on hormone therapy. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
o: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.e: Postmenopausal bleeding must be investigated for endometrial cancer, and transvaginal ultrasound measuring endometrial thickness is the first test; a thickened endometrium needs biopsy or hysteroscopy. Cervical cytology is a screening test and does not assess the endometrium.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has heavy regular periods affecting her work. Examination and ultrasound show a normal-sized uterus with no fibroids or polyps. Hb is 10.8 g/dL. She also wants contraception. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
